name: Finding Adjacent Consecutive Numbers in a Sequence of Integers
description: Construct a program that checks whether a sequence of integers, entered one at a time, contains adjacent integers that are consecutive. The user enters -1 to indicate the end of the input.\nNote that integers which follow each other in order, without gaps, from smallest to largest are consecutive numbers. For example, 12, 13, 14 and 15 are consecutive numbers.

comments.content: We prompt the user to enter the integer separated by spaces or new line. The user can enter -1 to quit.
We need to read and process the values that user enters. To read the input values from user, we need to define a Scanner object.

We can create a Scanner object using the operator new, as shown in this statement. The System.in object represents the standard input stream, which by default is the keyboard. It tells the java compiler that the input will be provided through keyboard.

Note that, unless specified otherwise, a Scanner object assumes that whitespace characters (space characters, tabs, and new lines) are used to separate the input values from each other.
We need to read the first integer that the user enters and store it in a variable. We read the integer by calling the nextInt() method because this input is an integer.
Note that if the user provides a non-integer number, an exception will be thrown because the input type is inconsistent with the expected data type, i.e., int.

We need to repeat receiving the integers from the user as long as the user enters an integer that is different from -1. Therefore, we need to use a loop structure. Since we don't know ahead of time how many times the loop will be repeated, we need to use a while loop. The condition in the while loop tests whether the body of the loop should be repeated, so it should test whether the input integer is different from -1.

The body of the while loop is repeated as long as the user enters an integer that is different from -1. The loop terminates when the loop condition evaluates to false, that is when the user enters -1.
We store the integer that the user entered in a variable called previous because we want to later compare it with the next integer that user will enter to check if they are consecutive numbers.

We need to read the next integer that the user enters. The call to nextInt() method returns the next integer that the user enters. Note that if the input consists of a sequence of integers separated by spaces or new line, each call to nextInt() method would return the next integer in the sequence.
Note that if the user provides a non-integer number, an exception will be thrown because the input type is inconsistent with the expected data type, i.e., int.

We need to test if the integer that the user entered is different from -1 because -1 indicates the end of the input and we need to skip it. We also need to test whether the integer that the user entered and its previous integer are consecutive numbers. To determine if the two integers are consecutive we need to test whether the difference between the two integers is 1 (consecutive numbers must differ by 1).

If the integer that the user entered is different from -1 and differs by 1 from its previous integer, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
Note that the && operator yields the result true if both conditions are true.
This statement prints to the default standard output stream, the two adjacent integers that are consecutive. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
The expression in the argument of the println method returns a string that is obtained by concatenating the given string and value of the variables.
We close the scanner as we do not want to process any input from the user in the rest of the program.
